# 📥 Getting the data in

## Import: the first step of the pipeline

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="The data science pipeline: import, then tidy, then a loop of transform, visualise and model, then communicate. The import step is highlighted: data import is the first step of the pipeline."}
#| label: img-data-import
knitr::include_graphics("images/fig-data-import.png")
```

In terms of the data science pipeline, every data science project starts with **getting the data into our software**. This step is called **data import**.

## In this unit

In this unit, we show **how to get data into R**:

-   We consider **two particular cases**: *delimited* files and *MS Excel workbooks*. Both are examples of **tabular data**, i.e. data that comes in tables.
-   We touch upon some **caveats** and illustrate the **arguments** of the importing functions that allow us to work around them.
-   We also illustrate how to **import other file types**, namely files generated by statistical software.

::: callout-note
## Disclaimer

Some data used in this unit is simulated.
:::

# 📄 Delimited files

## A table in a text file

In delimited files, the data entries are stored as a **table** in a **text file**: one row of the table per line, with the columns separated by a specific **delimiter character**, e.g. a comma (`,`), a semicolon (`;`) or a tabulation character (tab for short).

The delimiters give their **names** to the two most widespread file types: CSV (**C**omma-**S**eparated **V**alues, e.g. `data.csv`) and TSV (**T**ab-**S**eparated **V**alues, e.g. `data.tsv`).

## 

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="The same small table (name, gender, weight, height, bmi) saved in two text formats: team.csv, where the values are separated by commas, and team.tsv, where they are separated by tabs."}
#| label: img-delimiters
knitr::include_graphics("images/1-delim.png")
```

## CSV is the most common format for sharing data

CSV files are the **most common file format for sharing small- and mid-sized data** (up to several GB). Their main advantage is that they are **software-agnostic**: any program can read them. This is especially important if you work in a team. 

## `read_csv()` reads a CSV file into R

R has dozens of functions to import such files. We use the functions of the `{readr}` package, which is part of the `{tidyverse}`. The function `read_csv()` reads CSV files.

We need to give it the **path to the file**, on our computer or even on the web. It is convenient to **store the data in an object**, so we can use it later on:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#| label: read-csv-template
name_of_object <- read_csv("path_to_file")
```

## Example: reading `team.csv`

A file called `team.csv` is in the folder `data`. Inspect it by opening it first:

![](images/team_csv.png){fig-alt="The file team.csv opened in a text editor: a header line name,gender,weight,height,bmi followed by ten lines of comma-separated values, one per team member." fig-align="center" width="40%"}

In our case, the path to give to `read_csv()` is `"data/team.csv"`. We store the result in the object `team` and print it to have a look:

```{r}
#| label: print-team
# attach readr
library(readr)

# load the data
team <- read_csv("data/team.csv")

# print the data
team
```

# Useful arguments of `read_csv()`

## Where your file is: the `file` path

The first argument of `read_csv()` is `file`, the path to the file you want to import: *where on your computer is it?* It is given **as a string**, and it can be a local path (`"data/team.csv"`) or a URL.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Relative vs Absolute paths

In Quarto and R Markdown documents, paths can start from the **document's folder**. Our document lies in a folder that contains a `data` folder, where the file `team.csv` is found:

-   ✅ the **relative** path `"data/team.csv"`
-   ❌ an **absolute** path such as `"/Users/jack/Documents/my/unique/folders/data/team.csv"`

Relative paths work on **any computer**, so you can share the folder as it is. This is extremely beneficial, especially if you're **working with a collaborator!** The same code runs on their computer, whatever their folder structure.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
Paths start from the document's folder **only in Quarto / R Markdown documents**. In R scripts and in the console, they start from the *working directory* instead.
:::

## CSV/TSV data can be messy too!

Real-world files rarely look as clean as `team.csv`. They can lack a header, write missing values in their own way, or start with lines of notes:

![](images/team_meta_data.png){fig-alt="A CSV file opened in a text editor. Its first two lines are notes about the data, followed by an empty line, the header line name,gender,weight,height,bmi and ten lines of comma-separated values." fig-align="center" width="40%"}

`read_csv()` has arguments to deal with each of these caveats:

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.alt="A call to read_csv() with the arguments file, col_names, na and skip, each linked by an arrow to what it controls in a CSV file: the file name, the header row with the column names, the 'null' values to treat as missing, and the three lines of notes above the data to skip."}
#| label: img-read-csv-arguments
knitr::include_graphics("images/1-read_csv.png")
```

## When the first row is data: `col_names = FALSE`

Some data comes **without column names**. The file `team_wo_header.csv` is an example: its first row is already data.

![](images/team_wo_header_csv.png){fig-alt="The file team_wo_header.csv opened in a text editor: ten lines of comma-separated values, starting directly with the first team member, without a header line." fig-align="center" width="40%"}

By default, `read_csv()` considers **the first row** as the **column names**, so the first team member ends up in the header:

```{r}
#| label: raw-team-wo-header
team_wo_header <- read_csv("data/team_wo_header.csv")

team_wo_header %>% head()
```

The argument `col_names` defines **how to treat the first row**: if it does not contain the column names, we set `col_names = FALSE`, and R generates the column names `X1`, `X2`, etc.

```{r}
#| label: read-team-wo-header
team_wo_header <- read_csv("data/team_wo_header.csv", 
                           col_names = FALSE)

team_wo_header %>% head()
```

## Declare the missing values: `na = "null"`

In R, **missing values are denoted as `NA`**. However, other programs have other ways of declaring a missing value, e.g. `null`. Take a look at the `team_missing.csv` dataset:

![](images/team_missing_csv.png){fig-alt="The file team_missing.csv opened in a text editor: the team data, with the word null written in place of some weights and heights." fig-align="center" width="40%"}

When imported with `read_csv()`, these values are read as the **character string `"null"`**, and every column that contains one is imported as text, even if it holds numbers:

```{r}
#| label: read-team-missing
team_missing <- read_csv("data/team_missing.csv")
team_missing
```

Setting `na = "null"` is a lifesaver in this case: `null` is read as `NA`, and the numeric columns are numbers again.

```{r}
#| label: read-team-missing-na
team_missing <- read_csv("data/team_missing.csv", 
                         na = "null")
team_missing
```

## Jump over the metadata: `skip = 3`

Some text files have a **description of the data in their first lines**, sometimes called "metadata". The file `team_meta.csv` starts with three such lines: two lines of notes and an empty line.

![](images/team_meta_csv.png){fig-alt="The file team_meta.csv opened in a text editor: two lines of notes, 'The physiological data of team members' and 'Only for internal use!', an empty line, then the header line and the team data." fig-align="center" width="40%"}

Read as it is, the metadata gets mixed into the data:

```{r}
#| label: read-team-meta-default
team_meta <- read_csv("data/team_meta.csv")
team_meta
```

When importing the data into a tibble, **these lines must be skipped**. The argument `skip` tells `read_csv()` how many lines to jump over:

```{r}
#| label: read-team-meta
team_meta <- read_csv("data/team_meta.csv", 
                      skip = 3)
team_meta
```

## Handle special characters: `locale`

Files in a **language with special characters** (e.g. French, German, etc.) can come out garbled, because `read_csv()` guesses the wrong **encoding**. The file `cities.csv` contains two Swiss city names:

![](images/cities_csv.png){fig-alt="The content of cities.csv shown as a table with the columns name and population: Neuchâtel, 32819, and Zürich, 402762." fig-align="center" width="30%"}

Compare the output of the following code chunks. Setting `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")` reads the file with the `latin1` encoding, so the special characters are imported correctly.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: read-cities
#| error: true
cities <- read_csv("data/cities.csv")
cities
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| label: read-cities-latin1
cities <- read_csv(
  "data/cities.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
cities
```
:::
::::

## 💡 Use the ~~force~~ <kbd>Tab</kbd>

::: callout-tip
If you don't remember the exact name of an argument, move your cursor inside the parentheses and hit <kbd>Tab</kbd>. The function's argument list pops up: you can select the one you need and even read a short description.
:::

## Other delimiters, same arguments

Since `read_csv()` uses a comma (`,`) as a delimiter, it assumes that the **decimal mark is a dot (`.`)**. Otherwise, it would confuse decimal marks with separators!

-   In countries that use a **decimal comma**, the **delimiter is typically a semicolon (`;`)**. `read_csv()` has a twin sibling for these files: `read_csv2()`.
-   Two other functions, `read_tsv()` and `read_delim()`, read tab-separated files and files with any other delimiter.
-   Another nicety of `{readr}`: all the arguments we've seen are available in these functions too.

The table below summarises the `{readr}` functions and their delimiters.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: table-readr-functions
tribble(
  ~ `Function`, ~ `Delimiter`, ~ `Default decimal`,
  "`read_csv()`", "`,` (comma)", "`.` (dot)",
  "`read_csv2()`", "`;` (semicolon)", "`,` (comma)",
  "`read_tsv()`", "Tab", "`.` (dot)",
  "`read_delim()`", "Custom", "`.` (dot)",
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

# 📗 Excel files

## `{readxl}` reads Excel workbooks

MS Excel is one of the most popular formats for storing small datasets, so let's see **how to import data from Excel files**, usually with an `.xls` or `.xlsx` extension.

We use the `{readxl}` package. It is installed along with the `{tidyverse}`, but it is not part of its core, so `library(tidyverse)` doesn't attach it. If it is missing on your system, install it:

``` r
install.packages("readxl")
```

::: callout-warning
## Note

You don't have to do this on Renku, as it has been installed already!
:::

Once it is installed, we attach it:

```{r}
#| label: attach-readxl
library(readxl)
```

To read data from Excel into R, `{readxl}` has several functions. As with `{readr}`, the **first argument** is the **path** to the file.

| function | extension |
|----------|-----------|
| `read_xls()` | `.xls` |
| `read_xlsx()` | `.xlsx` |
| `read_excel()` | guesses the extension |

## Example: reading `team.xlsx`

Open the file `team.xlsx` (with MS Excel) and have a look at how it is structured:

![](images/team_xlsx.png){fig-alt="The file team.xlsx opened in Excel: a single sheet, Sheet 1, with the column names name, gender, weight, height and bmi in row 1 and one team member per row below." fig-align="center" width="50%"}

Then, let's import it into R and store its contents in the object `team`:

```{r}
#| label: read-team-xlsx
team <- read_xlsx("data/team.xlsx")
team
```

## Excel files are even messier!

Excel files are not always clean and tidy. For instance, open the file `je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx` and see it for yourself: it's an **Excel workbook** with several **sheets**, and the table sits somewhere in the middle of the **cells**.

![](images/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.gif){fig-alt="The workbook je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx opened in Excel, on its Women sheet. Rows 1 to 4 hold the title and notes, rows 6 and 7 the years and quarters, and the values by economic division start in row 9 and extend over many columns." fig-align="center"}

By the end of this section, you'll be able to get the data you need from this file. These are the arguments we use:

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="A call to read_excel() with the arguments file, sheet, range and col_names, each linked by an arrow to what it controls in an Excel workbook: the file name, the second sheet, the cell range C3:G23 that holds the table, and its header row."}
#| label: img-read-excel-arguments
knitr::include_graphics("images/2-excel.png")
```

## Which sheet to import: `sheet`

An Excel file (a workbook) can have several **sheets**. By default, `{readxl}` functions import the **first sheet**. The argument **`sheet`** controls **which sheet is imported**. It can be given as the **name of the sheet**, e.g. `sheet = "Women"`, or as **its position** in the workbook, e.g. `sheet = 4`.

![](images/je-e-06.02.00.01.02_sheet.png){fig-alt="The workbook je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx in Excel, with its sheet tabs Total, Seasonally adjusted total, Men and Women at the bottom. The Women tab is circled." fig-align="center" width="70%"}

Let's import the sheet `"Women"` from `je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx`:

```{r}
#| label: read-women-sheet
women_jobs <- read_xlsx("data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women"
)

women_jobs %>% head()
```

::: callout-important
## Wait!

The data has been imported, but it isn't usable yet.
:::

## Which cells to import: `range`

Specifying the `sheet` is not enough here: the table doesn't start at the top-left of the sheet, and the **data is all over the place**, so skipping lines (with `skip`) wouldn't help. Besides, we may be interested in only a subset of the cells.

With the argument `range`, we refer to a **rectangle of cells** by its **upper-left** and **lower-right** cells, separated by a colon (`:`). For instance, `range = "B2:K14"` imports the data in the rectangle between cells B2 and K14. In our file, the table lies between the cells A9 and DP72:

![](images/je-e-06.02.00.01.02_sheet_range.png){fig-alt="The Women sheet of je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx in Excel, with the cells from A9 downwards and to the right outlined: the block of values to import, without the title, the notes and the header rows above it." fig-align="center" width="70%"}

```{r}
#| label: read-women-range
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women",
  range = "A9:DP72"
)

women_jobs
```

::: callout-important
## Almost there!

We are one step closer, but the **column names contain values**.
:::

## When the first row is data: `col_names = FALSE`, again

The last step is to set an argument we already know: `col_names = FALSE`.

```{r}
#| label: read-women-col-names
women_jobs <- read_xlsx("data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women",
  range = "A9:DP72",
  col_names = FALSE
)

women_jobs
```

::: callout-important
## Notice the name choice

Unlike `readr::read_csv()`, `{readxl}` names the columns `...1`, `...2`, etc.
:::

# 📊 Files from statistical software

## `{haven}` reads SAS, SPSS and Stata files

Data might also come in a file format generated by statistical software, e.g. SAS, SPSS or Stata. Data from these programs can be imported with the `{haven}` package, which reads and writes `.sas7bdat`, `.sas7bcat`, `.xpt`, `.sav`, `.por` and `.dta` files.

The table below summarises which function to use:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: handout-table-haven-functions
tribble(
  ~ `File extension`, ~ `Software`, ~ `Function`,
  "`.sas7bdat`", "SAS", "`read_sas()`",
  "`.sas7bcat`", "SAS", "`read_sas()`",
  "`.xpt`", "SAS", "`read_xpt()`",
  "`.sav`", "SPSS", "`read_sav()`",
  "`.por`", "SPSS", "`read_por()`",
  "`.dta`", "Stata", "`read_dta()`"
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="The {haven} package imports files from statistical software into R: read_sas() and read_xpt() for SAS, read_dta() for Stata, read_sav() and read_por() for SPSS."}
#| label: img-haven
knitr::include_graphics("images/3-other.png")
```

## Example: reading a SAS file

For instance, let's import a SAS data file with `read_sas()`:

```{r}
#| label: read-mtcars-sas
library(haven)

mtcars_data <- read_sas("data/mtcars.sas7bdat")

mtcars_data
```

Since these file types are very specific, we won't cover each and every argument. However, you can always read the documentation, e.g. `?read_sas`!
